hints: The first letter of the label decides the dictionary order most. Can you replace a bigger letter you already printed with a smaller one, and still be able to print the bigger one later?
Greedy monotonic stack: drop a larger letter on top when it occurs again later in text. Track each letter's last index and whether it is already on the stack.

1. Store last[c] for every letter in text.
  2. Scan text; skip a letter that is already on the stack.
  3. While the top is bigger than the current letter and last[top] is after the current index, pop it and unmark it.
  4. Push the current letter and mark it.
  5. Return the stack as a string.

approaches.name: Brute force
approaches.idea: Try all subsequences, keep those with every distinct letter exactly once, return the smallest.

approaches.name: Optimal
approaches.idea: Single pass with a stack of letters kept in order; pop larger letters that can be taken again later.

explain: For text = "cdadabcc" the last indices are c:7, d:3, a:4, b:5. Push c, then d. At index 2 (a), d is bigger and appears again at 3, and c appears again at 7, so both are popped; push a. Push d at index 3. The a at index 4 is already kept, so skip it. At b (index 5), d is bigger but index 3 was its last copy, so it stays; push b. Push c; the final c is skipped. Result "adbc". Edge case: repeated letters like "bbaab" must not be pushed twice, which the used-array prevents.
recognize: Subsequence with every distinct letter once, smallest in dictionary order → greedy monotonic stack with last positions.
